title: Talon:
headline: An author gave years to a book. Talon gives the same effort back, and asks for the same respect.
story: Talon judges books for the Inside Literary Prize. He knows people put their heart and souls into every book, so he reads with the same care. “I want people to put effort into me just as I put effort into them.”

Then he says why it matters for people inside: being part of the conversation gives self-worth. His “degenerate” line is push-back against a label, not a description of himself. The video ends on hope: you can be more, you can do more.

Auto-transcript of 20260611WSPv00048.MOV (Talon, Washington State Penitentiary, 11 Jun 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels are automatic and sometimes wrong: the interviewer is off camera.
[00:00] Alright, can you introduce yourself and tell me how your relationship with reading?
[00:06] My name is Talon and we're at Washington State Penitentiary.
[00:11] And my relationship with reading originally was to escape Juvie Hall.
[00:18] And then as I came to adult prison, you know, it was really a sense of, I had a lot of lack of knowledge.
[00:26] I just didn't know a lot. And so that's when I turned to non-fiction.
[00:29] And that was really my biggest motivator was to start learning as much as I can, as quickly as I can.
[00:35] Because you got nothing left to do but to work out and read. So that's what I do.
[00:39] Absolutely. Do people tend to, oh no, no. What qualities make a book stand out to you as a judge?
[00:51] So when it comes to certain qualities that make a book stand out to me as a, you know, when I'm doing this judging,
[00:57] a lot of it is how well the writer writes.
[01:02] Because I'm not looking for the steel game, 30 pages on describing me how a tree sounds and looks and is in this forest.
[01:11] But being able to be descriptive, but also allowing me to stay hooked in the book.
[01:19] Because if it's written very plain, very simple, you're not interested in the story.
[01:25] But most part, I would say, especially when it came to this contest, this being my first one,
[01:33] it really was the content and how much it hit home to me.
[01:38] It allowed me to understand that there are not only so many similarities I have with those from different parts of the world,
[01:46] but so many drastic dissimilarities that I have with them.
[01:50] And it was just, I don't know, it was very eye-opening and very kind of inspiring to see that from two totally different worlds,
[01:58] even different time frames, I was able to connect with people in ways that I never thought possible.
[02:03] So it was cool, especially through a page, I wasn't even talking to an individual, so it was quite cool.
[02:08] No, no, that's amazing.
[02:11] So how has reading these books and being a judge changed the way you think about yourself?
[02:18] Well, when it came to reading these books and thinking about the way that I think about myself and being this judge,
[02:27] it really kind of gave me a sense of responsibility.
[02:31] We have a sense of responsibility when it comes to reading these books because it's not just read a book to pass the time.
[02:38] Time and effort and care went into reading or writing this book for years.
[02:44] They asked their family members, hey, can you give me feedback?
[02:47] The book publishers, even trying to get a publishing, people put their heart and souls into this.
[02:53] This could have been their 17th book or their first and only book.
[02:56] So it really made me realize that there is an importance behind every book.
[03:01] They're more than just a stack of pages with a colorful cover on it.
[03:06] And so it really gave me an importance of understanding that just as someone put as much effort into that,
[03:14] I want people to put effort into me just as I put effort into them.
[03:18] So I have to give the same to this book as the person put into it themselves.
[03:23] And that is the only way I can really truly fulfill myself as a judge, but let alone as a reader in general.
[03:29] Absolutely. I absolutely appreciate that.
[03:31] Why is it important that incarcerated people are part of literary conversations?
[03:36] I think when it comes to prisoners being a part of any kind of literary conversations,
[03:41] just as a general rule, it's important for incarcerated people to be a part of any conversation.
[03:47] It gives them kind of a self-worth, makes you feel like you are doing something worthwhile
[03:52] and that you're not just some degenerate that's sitting in prison and made a mistake and this is what you're always going to be.
[03:59] It allows you to see that you can be more, you can do more.
[04:03] And so giving them a voice when it comes to anything literary, it allows them to not only look within themselves
[04:09] and then give that voice and feel heard and seen,
[04:12] but allow them to see that they're capable of that in other aspects,
[04:17] you know, when it comes to the workplace or it comes to even just in their family.
[04:21] That, hey, I know I have something good to say and I know it's valuable because of these other interactions that I've had.
[04:28] Why not allow me to do it in these other spaces?
[04:31] And it really comes down to allowing an individual to see their worth within themselves
[04:38] and the most simplest of things of what did you think about this book and that's important.
[04:42] Alright, let me stop there.
